sections.markdown:
## C — Defensive driving and road rage: the five safe-driving habits, what defensive driving means, concentration, mirrors and blind spots, following distance, scanning, communicating, the safety cushion, merging, intersections, passing, other drivers' errors and avoiding road rage
Knowledge domain: how to drive defensively in Tennessee — the habits that keep you ahead of trouble, how to concentrate, check mirrors and avoid blind spots, how far to follow and how to test it, where and how often to scan, how to signal your plans, how to keep space ahead, behind and beside you, how to merge, cross and pass safely, how to absorb other drivers' mistakes, and how to avoid and defuse road rage.

FACT_ID: sec14-F01 | anchor: A02
Learning traffic laws and safe habits does not end with your license; drivers are responsible for keeping up with new laws, rules and safety practices for life. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec14-F02 | anchor: A02
Aim high in steering: look as far down the road as you can to pick up the traffic information you need for good decisions. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec14-F03 | anchor: A02
Keep your eyes moving: scan instead of staring, shifting your gaze constantly so you keep up with changing traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec14-F04 | anchor: A02
Leave yourself an out by keeping open space in front of your vehicle and on at least one side so you can escape a conflict. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec14-F05 | anchor: A02
Make sure others see you by using your horn, lights and signals to make eye contact with drivers and pedestrians. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0106]

FACT_ID: sec14-F06 | anchor: A03
Defensive driving means staying constantly aware of conditions, planning ahead, anticipating dangers and acting in time to avoid hitting any obstacle or vehicle. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F07 | anchor: A03
Driving defensively means expecting other people's errors and being ready to make up for them, while behaving predictably yourself so you do not confuse others. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F08 | anchor: A03
The manual calls courtesy and consideration toward others the most important driving attitudes and the key to safe driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F09 | anchor: A03
Concentration is one of the most important parts of safe driving, so daydreaming, sightseeing and distracting conversations have no place behind the wheel. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F10 | anchor: A03
Check your rearview mirrors constantly, and always check them before you change lanes. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F11 | anchor: A03
Stay out of other drivers' blind spots so that another vehicle does not turn into you. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F12 | anchor: A03
Expect the other driver to do the wrong thing, and have a plan ready to counter the mistake. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F13 | anchor: A03
Follow the two-second rule: pick a fixed object ahead and count one thousand one, one thousand two; if you pass it before finishing, you are too close and should slow down. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F14 | anchor: A03
On high-speed interstates, behind large trucks or buses, and in bad weather or poor visibility, increase your following gap to at least 3 to 4 seconds. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F15 | anchor: A03
Drivers take in about 90 percent of their information about the road and surroundings through their eyes. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F16 | anchor: A03
Defensive drivers focus their eyes about 10 to 15 seconds ahead, roughly one city block, so they see trouble early and have more time to react. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F17 | anchor: A03
Watch for exhaust smoke, brake or backup lights and turned wheels, which signal that a vehicle may pull into your path. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F18 | anchor: A03
Before entering any intersection, look left first because cars from the left are closer, then look right, then take one more quick look left. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F19 | anchor: A03
Check your rearview mirror about every 10 seconds to spot anyone closing too fast or tailgating, without taking your eyes off the road ahead for more than a brief glance. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0107]

FACT_ID: sec14-F20 | anchor: A04
Use your turn signal any time you change direction, including lane changes, turns, entering an interstate and pulling to or from the curb, even when no other vehicle is in sight. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F21 | anchor: A04
Keep a safety cushion of space in front, behind and on each side of your vehicle so you have an escape route in an emergency. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F22 | anchor: A04
Rear-end crashes are very common and are caused by tailgating, so keep at least two seconds of space ahead, with extra room at railroad crossings and when stopped behind a vehicle on a hill or curve. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F23 | anchor: A04
If someone tailgates you, move to the right lane if there is one; otherwise, once the way ahead is clear and a pass would be legal, ease off your speed gradually so the tailgater goes around. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F24 | anchor: A04
Never brake suddenly to discourage a tailgater, because it only raises your risk of being hit from behind. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F25 | anchor: A04
When meeting oncoming traffic on a two-lane road, keep a little right of center in your lane so you do not crowd the centerline. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F26 | anchor: A04
Split the difference between two hazards by steering a middle course, but give more room to the more dangerous one, such as an oncoming semi-truck rather than parked cars. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F27 | anchor: A04
Take hazards one at a time: when overtaking a bicyclist with an oncoming car approaching, slow down, let the car pass, then move left to give the bicycle room. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F28 | anchor: A04
You need a gap of at least four seconds to change lanes, enter a roadway or merge, and you should cross several lanes one at a time, never cutting across them all at once. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F29 | anchor: A04
Do not enter an intersection unless you can get all the way across, and never block it or leave part of your vehicle in a lane of approaching traffic. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F30 | anchor: A04
Passing at 55 mph takes about 10 seconds, so you need a ten-second gap in oncoming traffic and enough sight distance, and passing never allows you to exceed the speed limit. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F31 | anchor: A04
After passing, wait to move back into the driving lane until both headlights of the passed vehicle show in your rearview mirror. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0108]

FACT_ID: sec14-F32 | anchor: A05
When another driver makes a mistake, such as passing without enough room, do not make it worse; slow down and give that driver room to get back into the lane. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec14-F33 | anchor: A05
Aggressive driving includes tailgating, honking, rude gestures, yelling, speeding, cutting others off and even using firearms. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec14-F34 | anchor: A05
To avoid road rage, give driving your full attention, control your emotions and do not join a confrontation, even by honking or glaring. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec14-F35 | anchor: A05
Give an angry driver plenty of space, and do not take traffic problems personally; stay polite even when others are rude. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0109]

FACT_ID: sec14-F36 | anchor: A05
If a driver follows you, go to a police station or another public place where you can get help. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0109]

Misconceptions: slowing sharply does not teach a tailgater a lesson, it invites a rear-end crash; passing does not permit speeding; you do not swing back in as soon as you clear the other car's front bumper; looking right first at an intersection is wrong because nearer traffic comes from the left; answering an angry driver with a honk or glare is still joining the confrontation.
Mnemonics: aim high, big picture, eyes moving, leave an out, be seen; one thousand one, one thousand two; split the difference, one hazard at a time; left, right, left; you cannot control traffic, only your reaction to it.
Glossary: defensive driving means staying aware, planning ahead and acting early to avoid collisions; safety cushion means open space kept around your vehicle; blind spot means an area around a vehicle its driver cannot see in the mirrors; road rage means angry, aggressive behavior by a driver toward other road users.
Dynamic facts: none in this chapter's driving advice; the aggressive driving statistic credited to a federal agency is dated and must be refreshed from the agency before it is shown to learners.
